title: Grouping deeply
summary: GroupBy with element and result selectors, composite keys, groups inside groups, ToLookup versus GroupBy, and CountBy and AggregateBy.

steps.title: The other GroupBy overloads
body: Module 6 used `GroupBy(key)` and then a `Select`. `GroupBy` can do more of the work itself.
**Element selector**: choose what goes *into* each group, not the whole item.
l => l.Split(' ')[1]);     // element: only the message
**Result selector**: turn each group into a result in the same call.
One more thing that surprises people: groups come out in the order their key **first appears**. `GroupBy` does not sort.

code: string[] log = { "WARN disk", "ERROR db", "WARN cpu", "INFO up", "ERROR net" };
var groups = log.GroupBy(l => l.Split(' ')[0], l => l.Split(' ')[1]);
steps.explain: Groups appear in first-seen order (WARN came first), not alphabetically. Inside a group, items keep their original order too. The element selector put only the message into each group. Add `.OrderBy(g => g.Key)` if you need sorted groups.

steps.title: Composite keys
body: "Average grade **per course per term**" needs a key made of two values. Use an **anonymous type** or a **tuple**:
record Grade(string Student, string Course, string Term, int Score);
var byCourseTerm = grades.GroupBy(g => new { g.Course, g.Term });

This works because anonymous types, tuples and records compare **by value**: two keys with the same `Course` and `Term` are equal. An ordinary `class` compares **by reference**, so `new MyKey("Math", "T1")` twice gives two different keys, and nothing gets grouped.

steps.prompt: `KeyClass` is an ordinary class with no `Equals` override. What does the last line print?
code: class KeyClass(string dept, string level) { public string Dept = dept; public string Level = level; }
steps.explain: Each `new KeyClass(...)` is a different object, and a class without `Equals`/`GetHashCode` is only equal to itself. Every item gets its own group: 4. Tuples, anonymous types and records compare by value, so the two `(IT, Jr)` rows merge.

steps.title: Groups inside groups, and ToLookup
body: A group is a sequence, so you can **group it again**:
**`GroupBy` vs `ToLookup`**: they build the same shape, but
- `GroupBy` is **lazy**. It does nothing until enumerated, and it regroups **every time** you enumerate it.
- `ToLookup` runs **now**, once, and gives an `ILookup` you can index: `lookup["IT"]`. A missing key gives an empty sequence.
Use `GroupBy` inside a query you are still building. Use `ToLookup` when you will look groups up by key, many times.

items: Regroups each time you loop over it
Gives an empty sequence for a missing key
Can be followed by more lazy operators before anything runs

steps.title: CountBy and AggregateBy
body: Two very common groupings got their own shortcuts in .NET 9. They skip building the groups and keep only a running number per key.
// same as: genres.GroupBy(g => g).Select(g => KeyValuePair.Create(g.Key, g.Count()))

Both give a sequence of `KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>`, in first-seen key order. Add `.ToDictionary()` (no arguments) to turn that into a dictionary, or deconstruct each pair: `foreach (var (key, value) in ...)`.
`AggregateBy` is `Aggregate` (lesson 6) done once per key: a key, a starting value, and how to fold each item in.

code: var longest = genres.AggregateBy(g => g[0], 0, (best, g) => Math.Max(best, g.Length));
steps.explain: `CountBy` counts per key in first-seen order. The `AggregateBy` key is the first letter, it starts each key at 0 and keeps the longest length seen.

steps.title: Dictionary loops to CountBy and AggregateBy
prompt: The tests define `record Order(string Customer, decimal Total);`
These two methods are written with loops. Rewrite each as **one expression**, using `CountBy` in the first and `AggregateBy` in the second. No loops.
```csharp
static Dictionary<string, int> OrdersPer(List<Order> orders)
var d = new Dictionary<string, int>();
foreach (var o in orders) d[o.Customer] = d.GetValueOrDefault(o.Customer) + 1;
return d;
static Dictionary<string, decimal> SpendPer(List<Order> orders)
var d = new Dictionary<string, decimal>();
foreach (var o in orders) d[o.Customer] = d.GetValueOrDefault(o.Customer) + o.Total;
return d;
solution: return orders.AggregateBy(o => o.Customer, 0m, (sum, o) => sum + o.Total).ToDictionary();
template: var dojoOrders = new List<Order> { new("Maya", 30m), new("Omar", 60m), new("Maya", 45m), new("Lena", 15m), new("Maya", 5m) };
Dojo.Eq("no orders, empty dictionary", 0, SpendPer(new List<Order>()).Count);
hints: Both return a sequence of `KeyValuePair`s. `.ToDictionary()` with no arguments turns that into a dictionary.

steps.title: Sidekick: where the time goes, by tag
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk tags` shows how many tasks and how much logged time each tag has. Use `CountBy` and `AggregateBy`, no loops, no `GroupBy`.
`static List<(string Tag, int Tasks, int Minutes)> TagReport(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks)`
- a task with no `Tag` counts as `"(untagged)"`
- `Tasks`: how many tasks have the tag (`CountBy`); `Minutes`: the sum of their `LoggedMinutes` (`AggregateBy`, seed `0`)
- most minutes first; equal minutes by tag in ordinal order (`StringComparer.Ordinal`)
- read `tasks` once into a list first: it may be a query that is expensive to repeat
Example: `bug` on two tasks with 30 and 60 minutes gives `("bug", 2, 90)`.
Given in the tests, from your earlier Sidekick pieces: `TaskItem` with `Tag` (lower-cased, `null` when blank) and `Log(minutes)`.
starter: static List<(string Tag, int Tasks, int Minutes)> TagReport(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks)
return new List<(string Tag, int Tasks, int Minutes)>();
solution: static List<(string Tag, int Tasks, int Minutes)> TagReport(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks)
var minutes = list.AggregateBy(t => t.Tag ?? "(untagged)", 0, (sum, t) => sum + t.LoggedMinutes).ToDictionary();
template: TaskItem DojoTask(int id, string? tag, int logged) { var t = new TaskItem(id, "task " + id) { Tag = tag }; if (logged > 0) t.Log(logged); return t; }
var dojoTasks = new List<TaskItem> { DojoTask(1, "bug", 30), DojoTask(2, "chore", 120), DojoTask(3, null, 15), DojoTask(4, "Bug", 60), DojoTask(5, "review", 0), DojoTask(6, " ", 0) };
Dojo.Eq("by minutes, most first", new List<(string, int, int)> { ("chore", 1, 120), ("bug", 2, 90), ("(untagged)", 2, 15), ("review", 1, 0) }, dojoReport);
Dojo.Eq("every task counted once", 6, dojoReport.Sum(r => r.Tasks));
Dojo.Eq("equal minutes: ordinal order", new List<string> { "api", "zed" }, TagReport(new List<TaskItem> { DojoTask(1, "zed", 10), DojoTask(2, "api", 10) }).Select(r => r.Tag).ToList());
var dojoQuery = dojoTasks.Select(t => { dojoReads++; return t; });
Dojo.Eq("reads the tasks only once", 6, dojoReads);
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
hints: Sort the keys: `.OrderByDescending(tag => minutes[tag]).ThenBy(tag => tag, StringComparer.Ordinal)` and select `(tag, counts[tag], minutes[tag])`.
steps.explain: `CountBy` and `AggregateBy` give one pair per key without building the groups in memory. Reading the source into a list first matters as soon as two passes run over it.
